summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. A foreign government's official guidance records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to arrest gender and sexual minorities under broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions, which carry imprisonment, fines and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. The same pattern appears in the treatment of identity documents: a foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite carrying a passport marked female, indicating that corrected documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor, the practical exposure sits in the morality provisions rather than in a dedicated statute, and in a court that has shown it will disregard a foreign passport's gender marker. Arrest risk is documented but infrequently reported; the consequences of an arrest, including deportation and public charges of this kind, are severe.
tangentialFactors:
Bahrain's decriminalisation is exceptional within its immediate neighbourhood: it is the only Gulf state not to explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy, so regional comparison figures overstate the risk here and understate the residual risk that survives decriminalisation.

The direction of travel in the legislature runs against that exception. The February 2024 adoption of further moral legislation by the Council of Representatives gives authorities additional grounds for morality-based charges alongside the existing indecency and debauchery provisions.

Societal attitudes and treatment by authorities were examined by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in 2016, covering 2011 to July 2016, which reported societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities findings alongside its legal-status research.
localsOnly:
Same-sex relations are legal, but there is no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in law or policy.

Legal gender recognition is not available in practice: the courts have refused a first-instance application for recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare on Sharia grounds, and have refused to order the Ministry of Health medical-committee examination the applicant sought. The refusal blocks the administrative route to corrected documents as well as the medical one.

Recognition of relationships and of family status for same-sex and trans partners is not established under Bahraini law; the Wikipedia-sourced record notes recognition limits without specifying a pathway.

Residents face the same indecency and debauchery provisions as visitors, but without the option of departure: penalties include imprisonment and fines, and deportation applies to foreigners only.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two source baselines conflict on the fundamental question of legality. The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada record BHR105575.E (August 2016) reports that "according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain," citing Canadian government material of 14 July 2016 and Gulf News of 5 February 2011, while the Wikipedia infobox sourced to ILGA, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report the 1976 decriminalisation. This conflict is unresolved and is not settled by the sources in hand; the 1976 reading is the more consistently sourced of the two.

Sourcing for this jurisdiction is thin and partly remote. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for roughly a decade, including bodies of the United Nations and Amnesty International, so local media frequently serve as the only source of documentation, and many findings rest on second-hand reporting.

The scale of active enforcement is not established. The available material gives individual arrests and a general foreign-government statement that arrests are relatively rare, but no arrest totals, conviction rates or sentencing data for gender-based charges.

No sourced information was found on prison conditions for trans detainees, on access to legal representation, or on whether any administrative appeal lies against the May 2023 gender-recognition refusal.
